title: The dreamer is self-lit
hookLine: a king keeps asking what a person's light is, after the sun, the moon and the fire are gone
carry: the self is its own light
tomorrow: What's left when even the dreams stop?

lines: WHAT LIGHT DOES A PERSON HAVE?
AND WHEN ALL OF THEM ARE GONE?
cards: What light does a person have? King Janaka puts that to the sage Yajnavalkya in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and the answers come one at a time.
The sun, Yajnavalkya says: by its light a person sits, goes out, works and comes home. And when the sun has set? The moon.
And when the moon has set too? Fire. And when the fire goes out?
Speech: in the dark, a person goes toward a voice. And when speech goes quiet as well? Then, Yajnavalkya says, the self is his light.

teach.h: NO SUN, NO LAMP, AND YET A WORLD
teach.b: Why go there? Because Yajnavalkya is about to talk about dreaming, and dreaming is the proof. At night there's no sun, no lamp, no voice.

And yet a whole world shows up: streets, faces, a house you've never lived in that is somehow your house. What's lighting it? The text's answer, paraphrased: in the dream, the person becomes his own light.
The Sanskrit is svayam jyotih, self-lit. Then a passage worth hearing slowly.

teach.h: NO CHARIOTS, BUT HE MAKES THEM
teach.b: There are no chariots there, no horses, no roads, but he makes chariots, horses and roads. There are no joys there, no pleasures, but he makes joys and pleasures.
There are no ponds, no lotus pools, no rivers, but he makes ponds, lotus pools and rivers. For he is a maker. What is the passage after?

First, the dream as evidence. Yajnavalkya isn't interested in what a dream means; this isn't a dream dictionary. He points at the fact that dreams happen at all, that something keeps seeing when every outer light is off.
Second, the dreamer as maker. Every road in the dream was built that night, by the one asleep. Third, the turn back to waking.
If something in a person can light a whole world in the dark, the same light is there at noon, quietly doing the seeing behind the eyes.
That's where Yajnavalkya is steering his king: the self, atman, isn't one more thing you see. It's the light you see by.
And one honest note: this is the Upanishad's teaching about the self, not a claim about how the brain dreams. It asks you to notice something, not to accept a theory.

how: Vedanta teachers read Yajnavalkya's teaching on the dream as a pointer to the self as the light of awareness, and study the waking, dreaming and deep-sleep states together.

o: a code of dream symbols, each with a hidden meaning
a time when the mind goes dark and sees nothing
a state where the self lights its own world, as in dreams

games.q: a person's lights — tap the pairs.

s: in the Brihadaranyaka, the dreamer makes the chariots and roads he sees
there are no chariots there, no roads, but he makes them, for he is a maker.
Yajnavalkya explains what each dream means
he isn't reading dreams. he points at the fact that something keeps seeing in the dark.
the passage is a claim about how the brain dreams
it's the Upanishad's teaching about the self, asking a person to notice something.

games.q: you're Janaka. the sun has set, the moon has set, the fire is out and no one is speaking. what light does a person have now?
o: none: he sits in the dark.
games.why: the self is his light, Yajnavalkya says. then he talks about dreams, where a person sees a whole world with no outer light at all.

practice: Close the eyes and let whatever appears come and go, a color, a face, a room from this morning, without following any of it.
Then turn gently toward whatever is seeing them; don't try to find it, just rest in the fact that the seeing hasn't stopped. If you pray, rest in prayer there.

wordCard.voice: Sleep. In the Brihadaranyaka, the dreamer becomes self-lit, svayam jyotih, and makes chariots, roads and rivers where there are none. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit svayam jyotih: self-lit. Yajnavalkya's word for the person in the dream.

carryVoice: Your line: the self is its own light. Even with every outer light off, something keeps seeing. Rest well.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.2–6 (Janaka asks what light a person has: sun, moon, fire, speech, the self)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.9–10 (in dream the person is self-lit; no chariots, roads, joys or rivers there, but he makes them, for he is a maker)
